title: COROS Dura 2 Solar Review: Massive Upgrade, Sky‑High Price – Is It Worth It?
body:
A new generation of bike‑computer technology has arrived, and it arrives with a price tag that will make many cyclists pause. The COROS DURA 2 SOLAR, the latest flagship from the Chinese GPS and wearables firm, promises a brighter display, longer battery life and a suite of upgraded navigation features that aim to outpace its predecessor, the DURA 2. Early hands‑on testing by veteran bike‑packer Neil reveals a device that delivers on many of its claims, but also raises questions about value, durability and the direction of high‑end cycling electronics.

The most noticeable change is the 2.5‑inch solar‑assisted touchscreen, which replaces the modest 1.6‑inch LCD of the original model. The larger, high‑resolution panel not only makes map reading and data glance‑ability easier on long off‑road adventures, it also integrates a built‑in solar cell that extends the already impressive 30‑hour battery life to roughly 45 hours under moderate sunlight. In real‑world tests, the solar boost added an extra eight to ten hours on a mixed‑terrain ride through partially shaded forest canopies, a benefit that could prove decisive on multi‑day bikepacking trips where charging options are scarce.

Beyond the visual upgrade, COROS has overhauled the hardware architecture. A new Snapdragon‑based processor handles data streams from dual GNSS constellations—GPS and GLONASS—more efficiently, delivering sub‑meter accuracy and smoother route tracking even in dense urban canyons or deep‑valley passes. The device now supports Bluetooth 5.2, enabling faster sync with smartphones, power meters, heart‑rate straps and even smart helmets. Users can also tap into COROS’s cloud‑based route planning platform, which now offers auto‑generated “smart routes” that adapt to terrain type and rider fitness levels. For the hardcore endurance athlete, the DURA 2 SOLAR adds a suite of advanced metrics such as lactate threshold estimation and real‑time fatigue scoring, derived from a combination of power, heart‑rate and cadence data.

However, the enhancements come at a steep cost: the DURA 2 SOLAR retails for roughly $699, a 30 percent increase over the original DURA 2’s launch price. Critics argue that many of the new features—larger screen, solar assist, and expanded sensor compatibility—could have been offered as optional accessories rather than baked into a single, more expensive unit. Moreover, the device’s increased size and weight—now weighing 115 grams versus 95 grams—may affect balance on minimalist bike setups where every gram counts. Neil notes that while the screen is clearer, it can be harder to read in direct sunlight without adjusting the brightness, which drains the battery faster than expected.

The market context amplifies the debate. Competitors such as Garmin, Wahoo and Bryton have all rolled out mid‑range models that blend solid navigation with modest price points, while premium offerings from the same rivals focus on integrated smart‑watch functionality. COROS’s strategy appears to target a niche of ultra‑endurance riders who value ruggedness and autonomy above cost. The company’s claim of a “solar‑powered” device taps into a growing consumer appetite for sustainable tech, yet the actual energy harvest remains modest and dependent on favorable weather conditions.

Looking ahead, the DURA 2 SOLAR could set a new benchmark for durability and self‑sufficiency in bike computers, pushing competitors to explore alternative power solutions and larger displays. Whether the price premium will be justified will likely hinge on how quickly the solar charging capability proves its worth in real‑world, multi‑day expeditions. For now, cyclists seeking the most capable navigation hub will have to weigh the allure of a brighter, longer‑lasting screen against the heftier investment, while the broader industry watches to see if solar‑assisted wearables become the next standard or remain a premium niche.
